claims.text: Changing individual elemental concentrations by a few atomic percent around equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will alter lattice distortion.
Changing individual elemental concentrations around equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will alter its phase constitution or stability.
Small compositional changes in HfNbTaTiZr will produce measurable changes in yield strength.
Small compositional changes in HfNbTaTiZr will produce measurable changes in ductility.
Increasing Hf content generally increases the strength of HfNbTaTiZr.
Increasing Hf content generally reduces the ductility of HfNbTaTiZr.
The proposed initial material is an as-cast, near-equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy.
Arc melting is an applicable synthesis route for producing HEA ingots.
Vacuum arc melting can be used to produce HfNbTaTiZr ingots with controlled ±5–10 at.% variations in individual principal elements.
Room-temperature hardness and tensile or compression tests are proposed to compare the composition variants.
Atomic-size mismatch produces lattice distortion in HfNbTaTiZr.
Changing elemental fractions modifies solid-solution strengthening in HfNbTaTiZr.
Changing elemental fractions modifies local ordering, lattice strain, and phase stability in HfNbTaTiZr.
Composition-induced changes in local ordering and lattice strain influence defect movement and thereby mechanical behavior.
Hf is treated as a relatively large atom whose increased fraction slightly raises hardness and yield strength.
Decreasing Hf content reduces strength and improves tensile elongation.
A near-equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr ingot processed identically will serve as the experimental control.
Changing a constituent by more than approximately 15–20 at.% from the equiatomic ratio may form additional intermetallic phases and compromise the nominal single-phase structure.
Processing variations and minor impurities may affect the magnitude of the mechanical-property changes.
Absence of detectable hardness or ductility changes, or a yield-strength trend opposite to the predicted Hf trend, would falsify the hypothesis.
